# opencode-project-guard

[![run-tests](https://github.com/rojosinalma/opencode-project-guard/actions/workflows/run-tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/rojosinalma/opencode-project-guard/actions/workflows/run-tests.yml)
[![release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/rojosinalma/opencode-project-guard)](https://github.com/rojosinalma/opencode-project-guard/releases)
[![license](https://img.shields.io/github/license/rojosinalma/opencode-project-guard)](LICENSE)

An [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) plugin that refuses file and shell writes into another project's
territory. A guard names an *owner* directory and the *paths* it owns; a session rooted under the
owner passes, every other session gets a refusal when `edit`/`write`/`patch` target a guarded path or
a shell command would write there. Reads always pass, and when the shell parser is unsure the call
passes too — false negatives are acceptable, false positives are not. Next to guards, *rules* match
regular expressions against a tool call's command, paths, written content or Code Mode code and
either refuse the call or let it run with a warning appended, so a house rule can be enforced by code
instead of by prose. Any internal fault is logged and lets the call through, so the guard can never
break a session.

Configuration and design are documented in [docs/](docs/).

## Requirements

- [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) ≥ 2.0 (plugin API `@opencode/plugin` 2.x)
- [Bun](https://bun.sh) ≥ 1.4 (the runtime OpenCode loads plugins with)

The plugin has no runtime dependencies; `@opencode/plugin` is imported as types only.

## Installation

Clone into the global plugins directory and configure your guards in `opencode.jsonc`:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/rojosinalma/opencode-project-guard ~/.config/opencode/plugins/project-guard
```

```jsonc
{
  "plugins": [
    {
      "package": "./plugins/project-guard",
      "options": {
        "guards": [
          {
            "owner": "~/projects/infra",
            "paths": ["~/projects/infra", "~/projects/dns", "~/projects/proxy"],
            // optional: replaces the generic "what to do instead" part of the refusal
            "message": "Infra is changed only from ~/projects/infra. Describe what you need to the user instead."
          }
        ],
        "rules": [
          {
            "id": "no-self-upgrade",
            "tools": ["shell", "bash"],
            "match": ["/\\bopencode\\s+upgrade\\b/i"],
            "message": "The opencode binary is updated by the release pipeline. Report to the user instead."
          },
          {
            "id": "compose-reminder",
            "kind": "warn",
            "tools": ["edit", "write", "patch"],
            "on": ["path"],
            "match": ["/(^|\\/)(docker-)?compose[\\w.-]*\\.ya?ml$/m"],
            "allow_from": ["~/projects/infra"],
            "message": "If this service is managed by the service orchestrator, change it through its API instead."
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Without `guards` or `rules` the plugin loads and does nothing. All options are described in
[docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md).

## Usage

Nothing to run: once a guard is configured, every new session enforces it. A session rooted outside
the owner that asks to edit `~/projects/dns/zones.yaml` gets a tool error such as

```
[project-guard] `edit` refused: /home/me/dev/dns/zones.yaml is owned by the project at
/home/me/dev/infra, and this session is rooted at /home/me/dev/app. …
```

and the same line lands on the OpenCode server's stderr. Set `guards[].message` to tell the model
what to do instead (which API to call, where to file a request), and `"debug": true` to log allowed
calls as well.

Rules are checked after the guards. A refuse rule fails the call with the rule's message; a warn rule
lets it run and appends the message to the tool's result. `opencode upgrade` with the rule above gives

```
[project-guard] rule `no-self-upgrade` refused `shell`: matched "opencode upgrade" in command. The
opencode binary is updated by the release pipeline. Report to the user instead.
```

### Approval of the exact job

`unless_turn_tool` only checks that *some* call of a tool (usually `question`) completed in the current
turn. `unless_turn_tool_match` checks *what was approved*: the rule passes only when the option label
the user chose carries a token describing the same job the guarded call names.

```jsonc
{
  "id": "print-approval",
  "tools": ["execute"],
  "match": ["/\\b(print_library_file|add_files_to_queue)\\b/"],
  "unless_turn_tool_match": {
    "tool": "question",
    // run over the chosen option labels; the named groups describe one approved job
    "answer": "/\\[print file=(?<file>\\d+) plate=(?<plate>\\d+|-) printer=(?<printer>\\d+) copies=(?<copies>\\d+)\\]/",
    // the same keys, extracted from the guarded call's subject (the Code Mode `code` here)
    "code": {
      "file": "/\\b(?:library_)?file_ids?\\b\\W{0,4}(\\d+(?:\\s*,\\s*\\d+)*)/",
      "printer": "/\\bprinter_id\\b\\W{0,3}(\\d+)/",
      "plate": "/\\bplate_(?:id|index|number|idx)\\b\\W{0,3}(\\d+)/",
      "copies": "/\\b(?:copies|quantity|qty)\\b\\W{0,3}(\\d+)/"
    },
    "require": ["file", "printer"] // keys the call must name; default: every key of `code`
  },
  "message": "Starting a print needs the user's approval of that exact job in this turn. Ask first."
}
```

The agent puts the token in an option label (`Print [print file=340 plate=1 printer=1 copies=1]`);
only a chosen *option label* approves, a typed answer never does. Every key the call names must equal
the approved job's value, so `file_ids: [340, 341]` is refused against an approval for `340`. The
refusal ends with `Approval check: approved: file=340 …; call names: file=341 …` (or `no completed
question in this turn`, `code names no printer`, …), also available as `{detail}` in the message.

This condition **fails closed**: when the session context cannot be read, the guarded message is not
found or no call of the tool completed in the turn, the call is refused. And it only covers tool calls
the plugin sees: a `curl` from a shell to the same HTTP API is a `shell` call whose command text this
rule never inspects, so either add a separate `shell` rule for it or accept that it stays uncovered.

## Development

```sh
bun install
bun test
```

There is no build step: `index.ts` is loaded by OpenCode as is. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md)
for the layout, the test conventions and how to try a change against a live server.

## [Unreleased]

### Changed

- Docs and tests: the example approval rule's `file` regex also matches `library_file_id`, so a
  single-item queue call (`{library_file_id: 340, printer_id: 1}`) is compared like `file_ids`.

## [0.4.0] - 2026-10-16

### Added

- `unless_turn_tool_match`: a turn condition that passes a rule only when a completed call of the
  named tool (typically `question`) earlier in the same turn approved the *same job* the guarded call
  names. `answer` is a regex with named groups run over the option labels the user chose (a typed
  answer never approves), `code` maps each group to a regex that extracts the same key from the
  guarded call's subject text, `require` lists the keys the call must name. The rule passes when one
  approved job equals every extracted key, so a call naming two file ids never matches an approval
  for one.
- `{detail}` placeholder in rule messages; refusals and warnings from `unless_turn_tool_match` always
  end with `Approval check: <detail>.` saying what was approved and what the call names.
- Exported helpers `turnMessages`, `namedGroups`, `chosenAnswers`, `approvedJobs`, `extractKeys`,
  `matchApproval`, `resolveTurnToolMatch`; `RuleHit` carries the full `subject` text and the `detail`.

### Changed

- `unless_turn_tool_match` fails **closed**: an unavailable session context, a guarded message not
  found in it or a turn without a completed call of the tool refuses the call (logged). The plain
  `unless_turn_tool` keeps failing open. A rule may carry only one of the two conditions.

## [0.3.0] - 2026-10-16

### Added

- `rules` option: pattern rules that inspect any tool by name, next to the unchanged guards. Each
  rule has an `id`, a `kind` (`refuse`, the default, fails the call; `warn` lets it run and appends
  the message to its result), the `tools` it inspects, `match` patterns (`/body/flags` or plain) and
  a `message` with `{id}`, `{tool}`, `{match}`, `{directory}`, `{subject}` placeholders.
- Rule subjects: `command` for `shell`/`bash` (with the `workdir` as a `cd` prefix), `path` and
  `content` for `edit`/`write`/`patch`, `code` for Code Mode `execute`, `name` and `input` for any
  other tool; `on` restricts a rule to some of them.
- `except` patterns that ignore a match by its matched text, `allow_from` directories whose sessions
  skip a rule, and `unless_turn_tool`, which passes a rule when the current turn already holds a
  completed call of the named tool (fails open when the session context is unavailable).
- `tool.execute.after` hook for warnings, registered only when a warn rule is configured.
- Load-time validation: invalid rules are dropped with a `[project-guard]` warning on stderr.
- Log lines `refused <tool> by rule <id> …` and `warned <tool> by rule <id> …`.
- Documentation of rules in `docs/configuration.md` (options, subject fields, texts, examples) and
  `docs/SDD.md` (rules engine and rationale).

## [0.2.0] - 2026-10-16

First public release.

### Added

- `tool.execute.before` hook that refuses `edit`, `write` and `patch` calls whose target lies under a
  guarded path when the session is rooted outside the guard's owner.
- Shell write detection for `shell`/`bash` commands: redirections, `tee`, `sed -i`, `perl -pi`,
  `rm`/`mv`/`cp`/`mkdir`/`touch`/`chmod`/`chown`, `git -C <dir>` mutating subcommands and
  `docker compose` lifecycle commands (by `-f` file or current directory), with `cd` tracked per
  `&&`/`;`/`|` segment. Reads and read-only subcommands always pass.
- `guards[]` option (`owner`, `paths`, optional `message` with `{owner}`, `{target}`, `{tool}`,
  `{directory}` placeholders) and a `debug` option that logs allowed calls too.
- Fail-open wrapper: any internal fault is logged as `[project-guard]` and lets the call through.
- Bun test suite over the exported pure functions, run on every push and pull request.
- Documentation: `docs/configuration.md` (every option, refusal text, logging, caveats) and
  `docs/SDD.md` (design and rationale).

# Contributing

## Running it locally

The plugin is a single TypeScript file loaded by OpenCode on Bun; there is no build step.

1. Clone the repo into the plugins directory OpenCode reads:

   ```sh
   git clone https://github.com/rojosinalma/opencode-project-guard ~/.config/opencode/plugins/project-guard
   ```

2. Add a `plugins[]` entry with at least one guard to `opencode.jsonc` (see
   [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md)); set `"debug": true` while developing so allowed
   calls are logged too.
3. Start a new OpenCode session in a directory outside the guard's `owner` and ask the agent to edit a
   guarded file. The call must fail with a `[project-guard] … refused` tool error, and the same line
   appears on the server's stderr. A session rooted in the owner must pass.
4. Plugins are loaded per location boot: after editing `index.ts`, start a new session (or restart the
   server) to load the change.

## Tests

```sh
bun install --frozen-lockfile   # fetches @opencode/plugin for type checking only
bun test
```

The suite in `test/project-guard.test.ts` drives the exported pure functions (`resolveOptions`,
`tokenize`, `splitSegments`, `shellWrites`, `targetsOf`, `decide`) with neutral example paths under
the home directory. Every new detection rule or shell construct gets a case: one that must be refused
and one that must pass. The same suite runs on every push and pull request in
`.github/workflows/run-tests.yml`.

## Code style and layout

- `index.ts` holds everything: options, path identity, shell analysis, decision, plugin object. Keep
  the pure functions exported so they stay testable without an OpenCode server.
- `test/` holds the Bun test suite.
- `docs/` holds the documentation (see below).
- Two-space indentation, no semicolons, double quotes — match the surrounding code.
- When in doubt the guard passes the call. A change that could introduce a false positive needs a
  test showing the read-only form still passes.
- `@opencode/plugin` stays a type-only import; the plugin has no runtime dependencies.

## Commits and PRs

- Plain, descriptive commit messages in the imperative ("Detect `rsync` destinations").
- One logical change per commit; keep refactors separate from behaviour changes.
- Every commit is GPG-signed (`git config commit.gpgsign true`).
- A PR describes what the guard now refuses or passes that it did not before, includes the tests and
  adds a line to `CHANGELOG.md` under *Unreleased*.

## Releasing

1. Move the *Unreleased* entries in `CHANGELOG.md` into a new `[X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD` section and set the
   same `version` in `package.json`.
2. Commit, then create a signed tag `vX.Y.Z` and push it with the branch.
3. Create the GitHub release from that tag with the changelog section as its notes.

## Documentation

- `README.md` — what it is, requirements, installation, usage, development, license. Nothing else
  goes there.
- `docs/configuration.md` — every option, the refusal text, logging, caveats.
- `docs/SDD.md` — design: the hook used, how targets are extracted, the shell parser's rules,
  decisions and their rationale, scope, operations.
- `CHANGELOG.md` — one section per release, product-level wording.
- `SECURITY.md` — how to report a vulnerability; `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` — the Contributor Covenant.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md` — this file.

# Security policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Report privately through
[GitHub Security Advisories](https://github.com/rojosinalma/opencode-project-guard/security/advisories/new)
(the Security tab of this repository). Do not open a public issue. You will get an acknowledgement
within a week and a fix or a statement before any public disclosure.

## Supported versions

Only the latest release receives fixes. Update your clone to the newest `vX.Y.Z` tag before reporting.

## What the plugin does and does not do

The guard is a guardrail for an agent, not a security boundary for a host:

1. It runs inside the OpenCode server with that process's permissions and inspects tool calls only.
   It cannot stop a process the agent already started, a write performed by a sub-process or a
   command the shell parser does not recognise — by design an unrecognised command passes.
2. It reads no secrets, keeps no state and makes no network requests. Refusals are logged to the
   server's stderr with the target path, the session directory and the session id.
3. A bypass of the parser (a write that reaches a guarded path without a refusal) is a bug worth a
   report, but treat the guard as a safety net: file permissions and the OpenCode permission system
   remain the hard limits.

# Configuration

All options live in the plugin's `plugins[]` entry in `opencode.jsonc`:

```jsonc
{
  "plugins": [
    {
      "package": "./plugins/project-guard",
      "options": {
        "guards": [
          {
            "owner": "~/projects/infra",
            "paths": ["~/projects/infra", "~/projects/dns", "~/projects/proxy"],
            "message": "Infra is changed only from {owner}. Describe what you need to the user instead."
          }
        ],
        "rules": [
          {
            "id": "no-self-upgrade",
            "tools": ["shell", "bash"],
            "match": ["/\\bopencode\\s+upgrade\\b/i"],
            "message": "The opencode binary is updated by the release pipeline. Report to the user instead."
          }
        ],
        "debug": false
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Options

| key | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `guards` | `[]` | list of `{ owner, paths, message? }`; `~` expands in `owner` and `paths` |
| `guards[].owner` | — | directory of the owning project; a session whose root is under it is never blocked by this guard |
| `guards[].paths` | — | directories the guard protects; a target equal to or below any of them is guarded |
| `guards[].message` | generic text | protocol appended to the refusal; `{owner}`, `{target}`, `{tool}`, `{directory}` are substituted |
| `rules` | `[]` | list of pattern rules, see [Rules](#rules) |
| `debug` | `false` | log every decision (allowed calls too), not only refusals and warnings |

With neither `guards` nor `rules` the plugin is inert.

Guards are validated when the plugin loads: an entry without a string `owner` or an array `paths` is
dropped, non-string entries in `paths` are ignored, and an empty `message` falls back to the generic
text. Several guards may be configured; the first guard whose paths match a target decides.

## The refusal

A refused call fails with a tool error of the form

```
[project-guard] `edit` refused: /home/me/dev/dns/zones.yaml is owned by the project at
/home/me/dev/infra, and this session is rooted at /home/me/dev/app. <message>
```

where `<message>` is the guard's `message` or, when none is set:

> Do not work around it. Changes to this territory are made only from a session rooted in the owning
> project (or through the API that project exposes); report what you needed to the user instead and
> let them decide. This call will not be accepted again from this session.

Use `message` to tell the model the concrete protocol for your setup (which API to call, where to
file a request, who decides).

## Rules

A rule matches regular expressions against the *subject fields* of a tool call and either refuses
the call or lets it run with a warning. Guards are evaluated first and are unaffected by rules; a call
a guard refuses never reaches the rules.

```jsonc
{
  "id": "slug",                  // required
  "kind": "refuse",              // refuse (default) | warn
  "tools": ["shell", "bash"],    // required
  "match": ["/pattern/flags"],   // string or array
  "except": ["/^rc\\.local$/"],  // optional
  "on": ["path"],                // optional
  "message": "…",                // required
  "allow_from": ["~/projects/x"],     // optional
  "unless_turn_tool": "question", // optional
  "unless_turn_tool_match": { … } // optional, exclusive with unless_turn_tool (see below)
}
```

| key | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | — (required) | slug naming the rule in refusals, warnings and logs |
| `kind` | `"refuse"` | `refuse`: the call fails with a tool error; `warn`: the call runs and the message is appended to its result |
| `tools` | — (required) | tool names the rule inspects (`shell`, `edit`, `execute`, an MCP tool name, …) |
| `match` | — (required) | one pattern or a list; `/body/flags` is a regular expression with flags, anything else is a plain pattern compiled without flags; the rule fires on the first pattern that matches any inspected field |
| `except` | none | patterns tested against the *matched text*; a match whose text matches any of them is ignored and the search continues |
| `on` | all fields of the tool | restricts which subject fields are inspected (see the table below) |
| `message` | — (required) | appended to the refusal or warning; `{id}`, `{tool}`, `{match}`, `{directory}`, `{subject}` are substituted |
| `allow_from` | none | directories (`~` expands); a session rooted at or below any of them skips the rule |
| `unless_turn_tool` | none | tool name; the rule passes when the current turn already contains a completed call of that tool |
| `unless_turn_tool_match` | none | `{ tool, answer, code, require? }`; the rule passes only when a completed call of `tool` in the current turn approved the same job the guarded call names (below) |

Rules are validated when the plugin loads: an entry without `id`, `tools` or `message`, or with a
pattern that does not compile, is dropped with a `[project-guard]` warning on stderr. The other rules
stay active.

### `unless_turn_tool_match`

| key | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `tool` | — (required) | the approving tool, normally `question` |
| `answer` | — (required) | regex with at least one named group; run over every option label the user chose in a completed `tool` call of the turn, each match's named groups form one *approved job* |
| `code` | — (required) | object `key → regex`; every key must be a named group of `answer`; the regex extracts that key from the guarded call's matched subject field (named group of the same key, else group 1, else the whole match; first match, trimmed) |
| `require` | all keys of `code` | keys the guarded call must name; a missing one refuses with `code names no <key>` |

Only answers equal to one of the call's `options[].label` count; a typed answer never approves, even
when it contains the token. The chosen labels come from the completed part's `metadata.answers`,
with the result text parsed as a fallback. The rule passes when at least one approved job equals every
key extracted from the call (plain string compare: `340, 341` never equals `340`). Keys that are not
required and absent from the call are not compared.

Unlike `unless_turn_tool`, this condition **fails closed**: a failed context lookup, a guarded message
missing from the context or a turn without a completed `tool` call refuses, and the stderr line says
why. The refusal (or warning) text always ends with `Approval check: <detail>.`, where the detail is
`approved: file=340 plate=1 printer=1 copies=1; call names: file=341 printer=1`, `no completed question
in this turn`, `question answered but no approval token in the chosen option; call names: …`,
`code names no printer`, `session context unavailable` or `guarded message not found in the session
context`; `{detail}` in `message` substitutes the same text. A rule may carry either
`unless_turn_tool` or `unless_turn_tool_match`, not both.

The condition only sees the tool calls the plugin hooks. A shell command that reaches the same HTTP
API directly (`curl …`) is a `shell` call with a `command` subject, which an `execute` rule never
inspects: cover it with a separate `shell` rule or accept that it stays uncovered.

### Subject fields

| tool | fields |
|---|---|
| `shell`, `bash` | `command` — the command line, prefixed with `cd <workdir> && ` when the call has a `workdir` |
| `edit`, `write`, `patch` | `path` — the resolved absolute target paths, one per line; `content` — the text being written (`content`, `newString` or the patch text) |
| `execute` (Code Mode) | `code` — the JavaScript passed to the runtime |
| any other tool | `name` — the tool name; `input` — the input as JSON |

Because `path` holds one target per line, anchor path patterns with the `m` flag
(`/…\.ya?ml$/m`) when a patch can touch several files.

### Refusal and warning text

A refuse rule throws

```
[project-guard] rule `<id>` refused `<tool>`: matched "<text>" in <field>. <message>
```

A warn rule lets the call run and appends

```
[project-guard] rule `<id>` warning for `<tool>`: matched "<text>" in <field>. <message>
```

to the tool's result, so the model reads it next to the output. Warnings are only added to calls that
completed; a failed call gets none. When several rules match, the first refuse rule in configuration
order decides; the warnings of every matching warn rule are appended.

### Examples

(a) Refuse a shell command:

```jsonc
{
  "id": "no-self-upgrade",
  "tools": ["shell", "bash"],
  "match": ["/\\bopencode\\s+upgrade\\b/i", "/opencode\\.ai\\/install/i"],
  "message": "The opencode binary is updated by the release pipeline. Report to the user instead."
}
```

(b) Refuse a hostname pattern in commands and in written file content, with an exception:

```jsonc
{
  "id": "no-dot-local",
  "tools": ["shell", "bash", "edit", "write", "patch"],
  "match": ["/(?<![\\w.\\/~-])[a-z0-9-]+\\.local\\b(?![\\w.-])/i"],
  "except": ["/^rc\\.local$/"],
  "message": "`.local` hostnames are not resolved here; use `<name>.home.internal` instead."
}
```

Without `on`, the rule inspects `command` for shell tools and both `path` and `content` for file
tools; `rc.local` is a file name, not a host, so `except` lets it pass.

(c) Refuse a Code Mode call unless the user approved it in this turn:

```jsonc
{
  "id": "print-approval",
  "tools": ["execute"],
  "match": ["/\\b(start_print|add_to_queue)\\b/"],
  "unless_turn_tool": "question",
  "message": "Starting a print on the 3D-printer API needs the user's approval via the question tool in this turn. Ask first."
}
```

(c′) The same, but only for the job the user approved — the agent puts a token in the option label
(`Print [print file=340 plate=1 printer=1 copies=1]`) and the call must name the same ids:

```jsonc
{
  "id": "print-approval",
  "tools": ["execute"],
  "match": ["/\\b(print_library_file|add_files_to_queue)\\b/"],
  "unless_turn_tool_match": {
    "tool": "question",
    "answer": "/\\[print file=(?<file>\\d+) plate=(?<plate>\\d+|-) printer=(?<printer>\\d+) copies=(?<copies>\\d+)\\]/",
    "code": {
      "file": "/\\b(?:library_)?file_ids?\\b\\W{0,4}(\\d+(?:\\s*,\\s*\\d+)*)/",
      "printer": "/\\bprinter_id\\b\\W{0,3}(\\d+)/",
      "plate": "/\\bplate_(?:id|index|number|idx)\\b\\W{0,3}(\\d+)/",
      "copies": "/\\b(?:copies|quantity|qty)\\b\\W{0,3}(\\d+)/"
    },
    "require": ["file", "printer"]
  },
  "message": "Starting a print needs the user's approval of that exact job in this turn. Ask first."
}
```

(d) Warn on compose-file edits from outside the owner project:

```jsonc
{
  "id": "compose-reminder",
  "kind": "warn",
  "tools": ["edit", "write", "patch"],
  "on": ["path"],
  "match": ["/(^|\\/)(docker-)?compose[\\w.-]*\\.ya?ml$/m"],
  "allow_from": ["~/projects/infra"],
  "message": "If this service is managed by the service orchestrator, change it through its API instead."
}
```

## Logging

Every guard refusal is logged to the OpenCode server's stderr as
`[project-guard] refused <tool> <target> from <directory> (owner <owner>, session <id>)`. Rules log
`[project-guard] refused <tool> by rule <id> from <directory> (session <id>)` and
`[project-guard] warned <tool> by rule <id> from <directory>`; a rule dropped at load logs why. With
`debug: true`, allowed calls are logged as `[project-guard] allowed <tool> <targets> from <directory>`.
An internal fault is logged as `[project-guard] internal failure, letting <tool> through: …` and the
call proceeds.

## Caveats

- Without `guards` or `rules` the plugin loads and does nothing.
- OpenCode loads plugins once per location boot; a location that is already running keeps the plugin
  set and options it started with. Create a new session in that directory (or restart the server) to
  pick up a changed configuration.
- The shell parser is deliberately conservative: constructs it does not understand (`$(…)`,
  heredocs, variables in paths, scripts invoked by name) pass. The guard is a guardrail for agents,
  not a sandbox; see [SDD.md](SDD.md) for what is detected.
- Paths are compared after `realpath`, so a symlinked checkout and its target count as the same place.
- Rule patterns are JSON strings, so every regex backslash is doubled: `\b` is written `"\\b"`, a
  literal dot `"\\."`, a slash inside `/…/` `"\\/"`.
- `unless_turn_tool` fails open: when the session context cannot be read, the rule passes. It only
  checks that such a call completed in the current turn, not what it was about; use
  `unless_turn_tool_match` for the latter, which fails closed instead.
- Rules see the tool input as the model wrote it. A command assembled at runtime (variables, `$(…)`,
  a script file) is not expanded, so a rule can be evaded deliberately; it catches what agents
  actually type.

# Software design document

## Purpose

When several projects share one OpenCode server, an agent working in project A can reach into
project B's files with a plain `edit` or a shell command. Where B owns configuration that A must not
touch directly (rendered config, infrastructure definitions, generated files), that write is wrong even
when it works. `opencode-project-guard` turns such writes into a refusal with an explanation, so the
model reports what it needed instead of changing it, while sessions rooted in the owning project keep
working unchanged.

Design priorities, in order:

1. Never break a session: any internal fault logs and lets the call through.
2. No false positives: reads always pass, and the shell analysis passes whatever it cannot classify.
3. Clear refusals: the error says what was refused, why, and what to do instead.

## Architecture

One file, `index.ts`, exporting pure functions plus the plugin object as default export.

| Component | Where | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Options | `resolveOptions`, `expandHome` | normalises `plugins[].options` into `{ guards, debug }`, expands `~`, drops malformed guards |
| Path identity | `canonical`, `isUnder` | realpath-based "is X under root" so symlinked checkouts compare equal to their targets |
| Shell analysis | `tokenize`, `splitSegments`, `writesOfSegment`, `shellWrites` | turns a command line into the paths it would write |
| Target extraction | `targetsOf` | absolute write targets of one tool call (file tools and shell tools) |
| Decision | `decideFull`, `decide`, `rejection` | matches targets against guards and builds the refusal text |
| Rules | `resolveRule`, `subjectsOf`, `firstMatch`, `decideRules`, `ruleText` | validates rules, builds the subject fields of a call, finds the first counting match and formats the refusal or warning |
| Hook | `plugin.setup` | registers `ctx.tool.hook("execute.before")` (and `execute.after` when a warn rule exists) and applies the decisions |

The guards use a single OpenCode hook, `tool.hook("execute.before")`. It receives the tool name,
the input and the session id before the tool runs; throwing an `Error` there aborts the call and the
message becomes the tool error the model sees. Rules add `tool.hook("execute.after")` for warnings,
registered only when at least one warn rule is configured. No state is kept between calls.

`@opencode/plugin` is imported with `import type` only: the plugin directory may have no
`node_modules` of its own, and a type-only import is erased at runtime, so nothing has to be installed
where the plugin is loaded from.

## Data model / storage

None. The plugin holds the resolved options and the session directory in closure variables for the
lifetime of the location boot. It reads nothing from disk except `realpath` lookups on the paths it
compares, and writes nothing.

## Key flows

### File tools (`edit`, `write`, `patch`)

1. `targetsOf` takes the input's `filePath`/`path`/`file`/`file_path` and resolves it against the
   session directory (or the input's `workdir` when present).
2. For patches it also scans the patch text for `*** Update File:`, `*** Add File:`,
   `*** Delete File:` and `*** Move to:` lines, so every file a patch touches is a target.
3. `decideFull` skips guards whose `owner` contains the session directory, then refuses on the first
   target that is under one of a guard's `paths`.

### Shell tools (`shell`, `bash`)

1. `splitSegments` splits the command on `;`, newlines, `&&`, `||` and `|` outside quotes. `|` splits
   too, because `cat x | tee y` must expose `tee y`.
2. `shellWrites` walks the segments and tracks the working directory: a `cd`/`pushd` segment updates
   the cwd for the segments after it; a `cd` with no argument means the home directory.
3. `writesOfSegment` finds the write targets of one segment:
   - output redirections (`>`, `>>`, `2>`, `&>`), except `/dev/null` and fd duplications;
   - leading wrappers (`sudo`, `env`, `nohup`, `time`, `nice`, …) and `VAR=value` prefixes are
     stripped before the command is identified;
   - `tee`, `rm`, `mkdir`, `touch`, `truncate`, `rmdir`, `unlink`, `shred`: every positional argument;
   - `chmod`, `chown`, `chgrp`: every positional argument after the first;
   - `sed -i` and `perl -i`: the file operands after the expression;
   - `mv`, `cp`, `rsync`, `install`: the destination (and, for `mv`, the sources — moving a guarded
     file away is a write to it); `ln`: the link name;
   - `git`: the working tree (`-C <dir>` honoured) for writing subcommands such as `add`, `commit`,
     `checkout`, `reset`, `rebase`, `merge`, `push`, `pull`, `stash`, `clean`, `restore`, `tag`,
     `branch`; `log`, `diff`, `status`, `show` and friends pass;
   - `docker compose`, `docker-compose`, `podman compose`: the `-f`/`--file` and `--project-directory`
     arguments, or the cwd when none is given, for `up`, `down`, `restart`, `stop`, `start`, `rm`,
     `build`, `pull`, `create`, `kill`, `run`, `exec`, `cp`; `logs`, `ps`, `config` pass.
4. Targets starting with `-` or `$` are dropped (flags and unexpanded variables), everything else is
   resolved against the segment's cwd and handed to the same decision as file tools.

The tokenizer honours single and double quotes and backslash escapes; `$(…)`, heredocs and other
constructs stay opaque words, which can only make the detection miss, never block.

### Owner check

A guard never applies to a session whose directory is equal to or below the guard's `owner`.
Comparison goes through `canonical`, which resolves the longest existing prefix of a path with
`realpath` and appends the rest, so a symlinked checkout, its target and a not-yet-existing file
under either all compare consistently.

### Refusal

`rejection` builds the message: a fixed head naming the tool, the target, the owner and the session
directory, then either the guard's `message` (with `{owner}`, `{target}`, `{tool}`, `{directory}`
substituted) or the generic instruction to report the need instead of working around the guard. The
hook logs `[project-guard] refused …` and throws the message as the tool error.

### Rules engine

Guards answer one question: does this call write into a directory another project owns? Rules
cover the rest: house rules that are a pattern in what the agent types (a command it must never run,
a hostname it must never write, an API call that needs approval first). They are evaluated in the
same hooks as the guards, with their own data path.

1. **Subjects.** `subjectsOf` turns a call into named text fields: `command` for `shell`/`bash`
   (prefixed with `cd <workdir> && ` when the call carries a `workdir`, so a pattern can see where it
   runs); `path` (the resolved targets from `targetsOf`, joined by newlines) and `content` (the
   `content`, `newString` or patch text) for `edit`/`write`/`patch`; `code` for Code Mode's
   `execute`; `name` and `input` (JSON) for any other tool. `on` narrows the fields a rule reads.
2. **Match.** `firstMatch` runs each pattern over each field and walks every match, not only the
   first: a match whose text is covered by an `except` pattern is skipped and the search continues,
   so `rc.local` next to a real `.local` hostname still fires.
3. **Scope.** A rule whose `allow_from` contains the session directory is skipped, the same owner
   test the guards use.
4. **Order.** Guards first, unchanged; only a call no guard refused reaches the rules. Among the
   rules, the first matching refuse rule in configuration order decides.
5. **Before vs after.** Refuse rules run in `execute.before` and throw, so the call never happens.
   Warn rules run in `execute.after` on completed calls and append their text to the result: the
   call has already had its effect, and the model reads the reminder next to the output. The after
   hook is only registered when a warn rule exists, so configurations without one pay nothing.
6. **Turn condition.** A hit carrying `unless_turn_tool` is dropped when the current turn (the
   messages since the user's last prompt) already contains a completed call of that tool. The session
   context is only read when such a hit exists. When the lookup fails or the turn cannot be located,
   the rule passes and a `[project-guard]` line says so.
7. **Approval match.** A hit carrying `unless_turn_tool_match` collects the completed calls of the
   named tool in the same turn, keeps only the answers that equal one of the call's option labels,
   runs `answer` over them (named groups = one approved job) and extracts the same keys from the
   hit's subject text with `code`. The hit is dropped when one approved job equals every extracted
   key and every `require`d key is present; otherwise it stays, with a `detail` that names what was
   approved and what the call names. A missing context, a missing message or a turn without such a
   call keeps the hit (fail closed).

Invalid rules (no `id`, no `tools`, no `message`, a pattern that does not compile, an unknown `kind`
or `on` field) are dropped at load with a stderr warning; the remaining rules stay active.

## Configuration surface

`plugins[].options` in `opencode.jsonc`: `guards` (list of `{ owner, paths, message? }`), `rules`
(list of `{ id, kind?, tools, match, except?, on?, message, allow_from?, unless_turn_tool?,
unless_turn_tool_match? }`) and
`debug`. Full reference and the caveats in [configuration.md](configuration.md).

## Decisions and rationale

- **Fail open, always.** The hook body is wrapped; any exception other than the deliberate refusal is
  logged and the call proceeds. A guardrail that can take a session down is worse than a missed write.
- **Conservative shell parsing instead of a full shell.** A real parser would still not know what a
  script or a `$(…)` expands to. Detecting the common direct forms (redirections, coreutils, `sed -i`,
  `git`, `compose`) catches what agents actually type; everything else passes by design.
- **Owner is a directory, not an allow-list of sessions.** The session's root directory is the only
  identity OpenCode gives a plugin reliably, and "rooted in the owning project" is exactly the rule
  being enforced.
- **Refusal text addressed to the model.** The error is read by the agent, so it tells the agent what
  to do (report, do not work around); `message` lets you make that protocol specific.
- **Empty default guards.** The plugin ships with no opinion about which directories are protected;
  loading it without options is a no-op so it can be installed before being configured.
- **`import type` for the plugin API.** Keeps the plugin free of runtime dependencies and loadable from
  a directory that has no `node_modules`.
- **Rules next to guards, not inside them.** A guard is a path-ownership question with a dedicated
  shell parser; a rule is a plain pattern over text. Keeping them apart leaves the guard semantics
  untouched and lets a rule inspect any tool, including MCP and Code Mode calls.
- **`warn` exists because some rules are reminders.** Editing a compose file can be right or wrong
  depending on who manages the service, which the plugin cannot know. Refusing would be a false
  positive; staying silent loses the hint. A warning appended to the result keeps the call and puts
  the reminder where the model reads it.
- **`unless_turn_tool` fails open.** Its job is "ask before acting", checked by looking for a
  completed approval call in the turn. If the session context is unavailable, refusing would block
  legitimate work for a reason the model cannot fix, which breaks priority 1; the check passes and
  logs instead.
- **`unless_turn_tool_match` fails closed.** It exists for actions with a real-world cost (a print
  job, a deployment) where a missed approval is worse than a refused call; the refusal tells the
  model exactly what was approved and what it asked for, so it can ask again. Only chosen option
  labels approve: a typed answer is free text the model could have suggested, and the token is placed
  in the label by the agent itself, so the user's click is the only thing that moves a job from
  "proposed" to "approved".

## Current scope and non-goals

Today the guards cover the OpenCode tools `edit`, `write`, `patch`, `shell` and `bash` and the shell
constructs listed above; rules can inspect any tool by name. Both are guardrails that make agents
report instead of act; neither is a sandbox, and neither tries to stop a deliberately evasive command
(a rule sees the input as written, not what a variable or script expands to).

## Operations

- **Logs:** everything goes to the OpenCode server's stderr with the `[project-guard]` prefix — one
  line per refusal, one per warning, one per dropped rule, one per internal fault, and one per allowed
  call when `debug` is on.
- **Health:** there is no state to check; if the plugin failed to load, OpenCode reports it at location
  boot and no `[project-guard]` lines appear.
- **Upgrade:** `git pull` in the plugin directory, then start a new session in each location (plugins
  are loaded per location boot). Run `bun test` after pulling if you changed anything locally.
